  "text": "Martin took the kitchen clock to the shop beside the station.

“It loses ten minutes every day,” he said.

The repairer held it close to his ear, although it was battery-powered.

“How old?”

“I'm not sure. Twenty years.”

“A new movement would cost more than a new clock.”

Martin examined a tray of watch straps.

“That's all right.”

The repairer wrote his number on an envelope and put the clock inside, leaving the brass handle sticking out.

At home, a pale circle showed where it had hung. Martin wiped the surrounding tiles, but that only made the circle clearer.

For three days he looked up whenever he wanted the time. Then he fetched his phone from wherever he had left it.

The shop called on Friday.

“Nothing wrong with the movement. Battery contact needed cleaning.”

On the way to collect it, he bought two currant buns. The baker put them in separate bags without asking.

The repairer demonstrated the second hand.

“See? Going nicely.”

Martin paid in coins. There was enough change for the parking meter, but he had walked.

Back in the kitchen, he stood on a chair and fitted the clock over its hook. It hung crookedly. He adjusted it twice, then climbed down.

He made tea and opened one bag. The other he put in the bread bin.

At four, his neighbour knocked to return a dish.

“Have you got a minute?” she asked.

“Yes,” Martin said.

He moved the newspaper from the spare chair. While she took off her coat, he reached into the bread bin and brought out the second bun."
